title: Not yours to finish (Avot 2:16)
hook: the work isn't yours to finish, nor are you free to stop
tomorrow: at the end of a book, the whole room says one word. which?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a king who honored a teacher of two things, even after betrayal. Thank the teachers. Today, one of them talks fast.
screen: `THANK THE TEACHERS.` → `ONE OF THEM TALKS FAST.`

segments.voice: Noa's goodbye list is taped to her mirror: coffee with the cast, the lake one more time, return the library books, call the summer camp friends, write Saba a letter. Far more lines than days left. Last night she nearly tore it down: if I can't finish it, why start? Rabbi Tarfon, in Pirkei Avot, sounds like her list. The day is short, he says, the work is great, the workers are lazy, the reward is much, and the master of the house is pressing. Urgent, every word. And then, in the very next saying, the same rabbi turns around: it is not upon you to finish the work. Wait. Why would the man in the biggest hurry say that?
screen: `A LIST TAPED TO THE MIRROR.` → `THE DAY IS SHORT; THE WORK IS GREAT.` → `NOT UPON YOU TO FINISH?`

segments.voice: Read the whole saying and the puzzle starts to solve itself. It isn't upon you to finish the work, Tarfon says, and you aren't free to walk away from it either. Two halves, and they need each other. The first half takes away a weight nobody can carry: the work is bigger than one life, so finishing was never the measure. The second half takes away the excuse: since nobody finishes, nobody gets to quit because they can't. Put together, the urgency stops being panic. The day is short, so do today's part. The work is great, so you'll never be the last one doing it. Some readers hear in this the whole shape of a Jewish life: the Torah studied and never finished, the world repaired and never done, each generation picking up where the last one put the tools down. Moses on Nebo didn't finish either. That's the detail to carry from Tarfon: the man who said the day is short also gave everyone permission to leave work undone, as long as they don't leave it. And Noa's list? The point was never the last line. It's the next one.
screen: `NOT UPON YOU TO FINISH.` · `NOR FREE TO WALK AWAY.` · `THE WORK IS BIGGER THAN ONE LIFE.` · `DO TODAY'S PART.` · then, large: `KEEP GOING.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing from this path you want to keep doing after the summit: a blessing, a page, a candle, a question. Name the most likely thing that will get in its way. Then decide, plainly, what you'll do when that happens, and say the plan to yourself once.
screen: `ONE THING TO KEEP DOING.` · `WHAT WILL GET IN THE WAY.` · `WHAT YOU'LL DO THEN.`

segments.voice: Not yours to finish: Rabbi Tarfon's saying. The work is too great for one life, and you're not free to stop.
Your line: keep going, even with the list unfinished and the day short. Ten of fourteen. Onward.
